facts.raw_span: 2 days of left orbital pain
hypertension controlled with lisinopril
several months of epiphora without prior dacryocystitis
Visual acuity: 20/25 OD and 20/400 OS
Edematous, hyperemic left eyelids
Diffuse limitation in extraocular movements in the left eye
Normal intraocular pressure
Normal fundi on both sides
Left-sided lacrimal sac abscess with postseptal fat stranding largely limited to the extraconal space
Initial cultures isolated gram-positive cocci in chains; later identified as pan-susceptible Streptococcus pyogenes
Increased abscess size with globe compression
diffusion-weighted imaging showed acute injury to the entire orbital segment of the left optic nerve

concepts.why: The patient has a left-sided lacrimal sac abscess with postseptal fat stranding and cultures isolated gram-positive cocci in chains, later identified as pan-susceptible Streptococcus pyogenes.
The patient has edematous, hyperemic left eyelids and diffuse limitation in extraocular movements, consistent with orbital cellulitis.
The patient has visual acuity loss and diffusion-weighted imaging showed acute injury to the entire orbital segment of the left optic nerve, consistent with optic neuritis.
The patient has an increased abscess size with globe compression, consistent with an orbital abscess.

rationales.F03: Epiphora is a symptom that can be associated with lacrimal sac abscess.
rationales.F09: The presence of a left-sided lacrimal sac abscess is highly suggestive of lacrimal sac abscess.
rationales.F10: The isolation of Streptococcus pyogenes is consistent with an infectious cause such as lacrimal sac abscess or orbital cellulitis.
rationales.F11: The increased abscess size with globe compression suggests a severe infection, which is more consistent with lacrimal sac abscess or orbital abscess.
rationales.F12: The acute injury to the orbital segment of the left optic nerve is highly suggestive of optic neuritis.

frontier_selector.rationale: The presence of a left-sided lacrimal sac abscess with postseptal fat stranding and increased abscess size with globe compression, along with several months of epiphora, strongly supports the diagnosis of Lacrimal sac abscess.
